paragraphs: Swamiji pointed out a pattern that runs through every nation's history: the people who became great and strong were the ones who believed in themselves.

He gave a striking example. A young Englishman once came to India as an ordinary clerk. Short of money and troubled for other reasons too, he twice tried to shoot himself, and both times he failed. After that, he began to believe in himself. He became convinced he was born to do great things. That clerk became Lord Clive, who founded the British Empire in India.

Now imagine, said Swamiji, if he had listened to the priests and spent his whole life crawling about, telling God how weak and low he was. Where would he have ended up? Probably in a lunatic asylum. Swamiji warned that teachings which constantly tell people they are weak and worthless do real harm. He had seen their bad effects all over the world, and he felt children raised on such ideas grow up half-broken.

His practical advice was simple: believe in yourselves. If you want material wealth, work for it and it will come. If you want to grow intellectually, work on that plane and you will become an intellectual giant. And if you want spiritual freedom, work for that, and you will reach it: Nirvana, eternal bliss.
learn: The story you tell yourself matters. Humility is good, but constantly calling yourself weak is not humility; it is self-sabotage. Pick your goal, whether career, studies or inner growth, believe you can reach it, and then put in the work.
